statement: Within the top-8 RL directions, the first singular direction of each matrix carries the format and stop part: it cuts cap hits, and at large size stops the model boxing its answer. Directions 2-8 carry the part that raises right answers on finished problems. So rank-1 edits finish without adding right answers, removing direction 1 keeps most of the correctness gain, and overdosing direction 1 produces unboxed answers that are graded wrong.
claim: On hard328 problems where a cued-base sample finished wrong (boxed answer within the cap, graded wrong), the rank-1 edit (top-1 direction per matrix of the RL-Math 3.1 delta, 1x) is right no more often than a second cued-base sample, while the directions-2-8 edit at 1.5x is right clearly more often: direction 1 adds finishes, not right answers on problems the base already finishes.
why_only_this: None of the other top mechanisms splits the RL delta by singular direction. The sampling mechanisms (round-09/grader-m01, run-08/f2-m01) only predict regression to the mean on selected problems, and that is the same for every edit; the second base sample removes it. The cap and grader mechanisms (run-08/f2-m02, round-09/grader-m06, run-08/f2-m06, round-09/training-m01, run-04/f2-m05) are about how unfinished or misplaced answers are scored, so they predict nothing about base-finished-wrong problems. round-09/grader-m04 and round-10/problems-m04 predict that an edit's right-answer gain sits on mid-difficulty problems and its cap change sits in the long tail, but they give no reason why direction 1 should have no right-answer gain while directions 2-8 have one. Under any of them, an edit that lifts the hard328 total by 17 (181 vs 164) should also raise the right rate on finished-wrong problems in rough proportion. Only this mechanism predicts a near-zero gain for direction 1 next to a clear gain for directions 2-8 on the same problems.
computation: 1) Load per-problem hard328 rows (problem index 0-327, right under grader v3, cap hit / finished flag, tokens, extracted answer) for these cells: (a) selector: cued base, T 1.0, sample 0, results/day1/hard328_base_cue_t10-01 (164 right, 77 cap hits); (b) second base: the four samples in results/day1_3/hard328_base_cue_s4r2-01; (c) TOP1: base + 1 direction per matrix of the RL-Math delta at 1x (posted 181/328, cap hits 51), its run folder under results/xreward/edits; (d) D28: base + directions 2-8 at 1.5x (posted 183/328, cap hits 69), its folder under results/xreward/depth3 or results/xreward/edits; (e) references: top-8 at 1.5x and matched random rank-8 (158/328) from results/xreward/edits, plus TOP1 at 2x (184/328) if it is stored. If a cell's per-problem rows are not in its run folder, take them from results/table/hard328-02 (per-problem rows of every committed configuration). Before going on, check that each cell's right count and cap-hit count match the posted numbers; stop and report any mismatch. Use studies/theory/results/direct/dial-01 (readout.json, m1x_hard328_rows.jsonl) as the template for the row format and for how 'finished wrong' was defined in result-124593, and use the same definition. 2) For each of the four second-base samples, compare its text hash or tokens and its answer to the selector row. Drop any sample that is the same draw as the selector. 3) Set S = the problems where the selector row finished (no cap hit, an answer extracted) and is graded wrong. Report |S| (expected about 87). 4) For each problem i in S, set b_i = the mean right indicator over the remaining second-base samples, t_i = the TOP1 right indicator, d_i = the D28 right indicator. Count a capped edit row as wrong. 5) Compute E_top1 = 100*mean(t_i - b_i) and E_d28 = 100*mean(d_i - b_i) in points, and G = E_d28 - E_top1. Compute each the same way for the top-8 1.5x reference (it should reproduce about +13.5 from result-124593), for the random rank-8 control and, if stored, for TOP1 2x. 6) Get 95% intervals from a paired bootstrap over the problems in S: 10,000 resamples, numpy default_rng(seed=0), percentile intervals, with E_top1, E_d28 and G computed on the same resample. 7) Repeat for every selector-sample pair as a robustness check: each of the 4+1 base samples serves as selector in turn, the others serve as second base, and problems are pooled with a cluster bootstrap by problem. Report it, but the verdict uses step 6. 8) Also report the finished-row precision (right / finished) of base, TOP1, D28 over all 328 problems, and the number of TOP1 rows with no boxed answer, as context only.
refuted_if: The rank-1 edit itself adds right answers on base-finished-wrong problems: the lower end of the 95% interval of E_top1 is at least the threshold. The claim is also refuted if directions 2-8 do not beat direction 1 on these problems: the upper end of the 95% interval of G = E_d28 - E_top1 is at or below 0.
threshold: E_top1 95% lower bound >= +5.0 points (refutes); or G 95% upper bound <= 0.0 points (refutes). The claim holds if neither happens and the E_top1 point estimate is below half the E_d28 point estimate.
null: The second cued-base sample on the same selected problems. It removes regression to the mean and is stronger than a random baseline. As a second null, the matched random rank-8 edit run through the same computation must give an excess near 0. As a positive control, the top-8 1.5x edit must reproduce about +13.5 points (result-124593). The contrast that decides is TOP1 against directions 2-8, two edits built from the same RL delta.

statement: A count 'at 16,384' rescored from a 32k run is a different measurement from a native 16k run: rows longer than 16,384 count wrong, while a native run lets grader v3 credit a box already written inside a truncated row (RL 69 % of capped rows, base 17 %, Think-SFT rarely). So 32k-minus-16k is extension finishes only, and models that box mid-reasoning lose a few problems when rescored.
claim: In native 16,384-cap hard328 runs, grader v3 credits a right answer to a real share of the rows that hit the cap (a box written before the cut): for RL plain at least 10 % of its cap-hit rows, more than Think-SFT's share. The 32k-rescored-at-16,384 count scores every such row wrong by construction.
why_only_this: round-09/grader-m06 says a count at a cap scores every unfinished answer wrong, and that rescoring 32k text at 16,384 reproduces a 16k run. That implies about 0 right among native cap-hit rows and no gap between native and rescored counts. run-08/f2-m06 treats a cap hit as an abstention that casts no vote, so it also predicts no credited answers there. The seed-noise mechanisms (grader-m01, f2-m01) predict scatter around equal native and rescored means, with no cap-hit rows credited. weights-m06, problems-m04, grader-m04, training-m01 and f2-m05 are about directions, strata, difficulty mix, template and drift. None of them says a truncated row can hold a box that v3 grades right. Only f2-m02 predicts credited cap-hit rows, and it predicts their order: RL (box in 69 % of capped rows) > base (17 %) > Think-SFT (rarely).
computation: 1) In each native 16,384-cap folder, load every row of rows.jsonl (problem index, sample index, tokens, finish reason or cap flag, v3 right flag, text if present). Use the 4-sample day1_3 folders for RL plain and base cue, the 4-sample thinkvote folder for Think-SFT cue, and the day1 single-sample folders as a check. A row is a cap hit if finish_reason == 'length' or a cap/cut-off flag is true. If neither field exists, use generated tokens >= 16,384. Before going on, check that the folder's cap-hit count per sample matches its metrics.json; for day1 RL the stated count is 20, for day1 base 77. 2) For each model, count H = cap-hit rows and C = cap-hit rows that grader v3 marks right. If the stored right flag is missing, re-grade the stored text with grader/rln4_grader_v3.py against the hard328 answer key in data/rln3/hard.json. Report C/H with a Wilson 95 % interval. 3) Where text is stored, check each credited row: its last \boxed{...} must sit inside the generated text, which ends at the cap. Report the share of cap-hit rows that hold any \boxed at all (the mechanism states 69 % RL, 17 % base, rare Think-SFT). 4) Compute RL share minus Think-SFT share, and RL share minus base share. Get 95 % intervals from a bootstrap over problems: 10,000 resamples of the 328 problem indices, all samples of a drawn problem kept together, seed 0. 5) Consistency check on the 32k rows (cap32 rows-01, rows-02). For each model, every row with tokens > 16,384 has right_at_16384 = false, so the rescore credits 0 of them. If token ids or text and a tokenizer are stored, cut each such row at token 16,384, grade the cut text with v3, and report how many it would credit. This is the same quantity measured on the 32k text.
refuted_if: RL plain's native-16k cap-hit rows are almost never credited: the Wilson 95 % upper bound of C/H is below 10 %. Or RL's credited share is not above Think-SFT's: the bootstrap 95 % upper bound of (RL share - Think-SFT share) is at or below 0.
threshold: RL plain C/H Wilson upper bound < 0.10 refutes. The claim holds only if the RL C/H point estimate is >= 0.10 and the lower bound of the RL - Think-SFT difference is > 0. If the lower bound is <= 0 but the upper bound is > 0, the result is undecided.
null: The ordering is set by each model's own cap-hit rows, not by chance. Primary null: Think-SFT cue's native-16k cap-hit rows (same set and cap, a model that rarely boxes mid-reasoning), with RL plain required to beat them. Secondary null: the base cue's cap-hit rows across its 4 day1_3 samples, with sample 0 against samples 1-3 giving a second-base-sample check of scatter. Rival null (grader-m06): credited share = 0, which the rescored 32k rows (cap32) show by construction.

statement: Each posted single cell is one seeded draw: new seeds on the same weights scatter by 5-7 problems per 500 and up to 9-19 per 328, and cells picked as notable (best size, first run) sit above their model's mean. Multi-sample means regress to the pooled level of near-identical cells: step-100 plain pools with step-100 cue (same opening policy), and the 164-problem references come from draws above their own 4-sample means.
claim: At RL step 100 the cue adds nothing beyond seed scatter on MATH-500: pooling all stored samples per arm, the paired per-problem difference in right answers between step-100 cue and step-100 plain is zero, so the 9-problem single-cell gap (427 vs 418) is a draw difference, not a cue effect.
why_only_this: Only round-09/grader-m01 says step-100 plain and step-100 cue are near-identical cells sharing one opening policy, so they pool to one level. run-08/f2-m01 shares the seed-scatter idea but shrinks each cell toward a structural prior that explicitly includes a cue effect, so it expects a positive cue gap to remain after pooling. round-09/grader-m04 says the opening moves few problems only on hard items; MATH-500 is mostly easy-to-mid items, where it expects the cue to keep moving problems. round-09/training-m01 and run-04/f2-m05 are about Think-SFT's template and drift on raw-template cue runs; they say the cue changes how answers end or drift, not that it does nothing at step 100. round-10/weights-m06, round-10/problems-m04, run-08/f2-m02, run-08/f2-m06 and round-09/grader-m06 are about weight directions, caps, votes and set strata, and none of them implies a zero cue effect on a step-100 checkpoint.
computation: 1) In each of the four run folders, read the per-problem row file (rows.jsonl; if it is missing, use the per-row records the folder holds). For each row, keep problem index (0-499), sample/seed id and right under grader v3. Use the stored v3 'right' field and do not regrade. 2) Assign arms: PLAIN = rows from s0100_plain-01 and s0100_plain_s123-01; CUE = rows from s0100_cue-01 and s0100_cue_s123-01. Count samples per problem per arm; the expected count is 4 per arm. Keep only problems with the same number k>=2 of samples in both arms, and report how many are dropped. 3) Sanity check: total right over all samples must reproduce result-6832a8 (PLAIN 1670/2000, CUE 1704/2000) and the per-folder counts in readout3.json. If either is off by more than 2, stop and report the mismatch instead of a verdict. 4) For each problem i, compute pc_i = mean right over CUE samples and pp_i = mean right over PLAIN samples, then d_i = pc_i - pp_i. The statistic is D = sum_i d_i, in problems per 500 (500 * mean d_i if fewer problems survive). 5) Paired bootstrap: resample the 500 problems with replacement, 10,000 times, numpy default_rng(0), and recompute D each time. Report D and its 2.5/97.5 percentiles. 6) Null A, label permutation: for each problem pool its 2k samples (k CUE + k PLAIN), then randomly reassign k to 'CUE' and k to 'PLAIN' independently per problem. Do this 10,000 times with rng(1), recompute D each time, and report the two-sided p = share of |D_perm| >= |D|. 7) Null B, second sample of the same weights: compute the same paired statistic within each arm between its two seed folders (s0100_plain-01 vs s0100_plain_s123-01; s0100_cue-01 vs s0100_cue_s123-01), scaled to per 500. Report both values next to D, together with the between-arm difference using one folder each (s0100_cue-01 vs s0100_plain-01; s0100_cue_s123-01 vs s0100_plain_s123-01). 8) Also report D separately on problems where both arms are 'mixed' (0 < pc_i+pp_i < 2), as a descriptive line only. 9) Verdict: apply refuted_if.
refuted_if: The pooled cue-minus-plain gap at step 100 is reliably positive: the lower end of the paired 95% bootstrap interval of D is above the threshold AND the label-permutation two-sided p < 0.05.
threshold: Lower 95% bound of D > 0.0 problems per 500 (with permutation p < 0.05) refutes. If the lower bound is <= 0.0, the claim holds, and the posted single-cell gap of 9 counts as seed scatter.
null: Sample-level null at the same checkpoint: (A) per-problem permutation of cue/plain labels across the pooled samples of the step-100 weights, and (B) the seed-to-seed difference within each arm (plain seed 0 vs plain seed 123, cue seed 0 vs cue seed 123), which is a second sample of the same weights and prompt. The cue gap must be no larger than what (A) and (B) produce.

statement: A cap hit casts no vote: a model that runs out of tokens abstains instead of guessing, so its vote approaches pass@k (Think-SFT 241 against 244), while a model that finishes long and wrong spends votes on scattered wrong answers (RL 221 against 240). Turning abstentions into finishes (larger cap, RL directions, transplant) raises single-sample counts more than vote counts, because most converted rows are wrong and dilute the right minority.
claim: On hard328, letting Think-SFT's 16,384-token cap hits finish (its 32,768-cap rows) inside a 4-sample vote turns at least 2 problems the vote had right into wrong ones, because the converted wrong answers now vote against a right minority, while the vote gains less than half of the 23-problem single-sample gain.
why_only_this: Only this mechanism says a cap hit's value to the vote is that it abstains, so turning it into a finished (mostly wrong) answer costs vote-right problems. round-09/grader-m06 and run-08/f2-m02 say how many cap hits turn right when the cap is raised (yield) and how a rescored count differs from a native one. They say nothing about votes, so they predict no flips and a vote gain limited only by the ceiling. run-04/f2-m05 says drifted continuations are wrong, not that they dilute a vote. round-09/grader-m04 compares sets (fresh2026 against hard328), not abstaining against finishing on the same rows. round-09/grader-m01 and run-08/f2-m01 are about seed scatter, round-09/training-m01 is about template answer placement, and round-10/weights-m06 and round-10/problems-m04 are about edit directions and problem strata. None of these predicts that a finished wrong answer takes a right vote away.
computation: 1) Load the Think-SFT + cue cap-32,768 hard328 rows: the per-problem rows in cap32/rows-01 or rows-02, whichever holds the Think-SFT cue arm, or sft_cue-01. Each row needs the problem index, generated tokens, finished or capped, the extracted final answer and right under grader v3. Check that you get 230 right at 32k and 207 when rescored at 16,384 (a row longer than 16,384 tokens counts as a cap hit there). Stop and report if either total does not match. 2) Load thinkvote/hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01/rows.jsonl (4 samples per problem, cap 16,384) and keep samples 1, 2 and 3. Drop sample 0 so that no draw is used twice. 3) For each of the 328 problems, build two 4-vote sets that share samples 1-3. In set A the 4th vote is the cap32 row scored at 16,384: if it is longer than 16,384 tokens it abstains, otherwise it votes its extracted answer. In set B the 4th vote is the same row scored at 32,768: it abstains only if it hit 32,768, otherwise it votes its answer. Rows with no extracted answer abstain in both sets. 4) Vote rule: plurality over the non-abstaining answers. Group answers as equivalent when math-verify 0.9.0 (as in tools/finding_imitation_beats_rl.py) judges them equal, otherwise by exact normalized string. Break ties toward the shortest finished sample. If all 4 abstain, the problem is wrong. A problem is right if the winning group is graded right by v3. 5) Report: G1 = right(row at 32k) - right(row at 16k), about 23. VA = vote-right count in A. VB = vote-right count in B. The vote gain is VB - VA. The converted rows are those capped at 16,384 and finished by 32,768. Count U = problems wrong in A and right in B. Count D = problems right in A and wrong in B. A converted row can only change the vote on its own problem, so every flip is caused by one converted row. For each D problem, record the converted answer, the answers of samples 1-3, and whether the flip came from a plurality or a tie-break. 6) Null A' (abstention): set B, but each converted row that is wrong abstains. This is the ceiling-only prediction of a pure yield mechanism. By construction its D is 0, and VA' - VA gives the ceiling-limited gain. 7) Second-sample null for scatter: among wrong finished answers, compare how often a converted 16k->32k row's answer matches one of samples 1-3 against how often a sample-1 row that finished under 16,384 and was wrong matches samples 2-3. Use Wilson intervals. 8) Repeat steps 1-6 for RL plain, using cap32/rl_plain-01 as the 4th vote and samples 1-3 of day1_3/hard328_rl_plain_s4r2-01, as a contrast. RL has 20 cap hits, so expect a smaller G1. Bootstrap VB - VA and (VB - VA)/G1 over problems, 10,000 resamples, seed 0.
refuted_if: For Think-SFT, D <= 1 (converted wrong rows flip at most one vote-right problem), or the vote gain VB - VA is at least half of G1 (the 95 % bootstrap lower bound of (VB - VA)/G1 >= 0.5), or VB >= VA' (letting the wrong converted rows vote costs nothing against the abstention null).
threshold: Holds only if D >= 2, the upper end of the 95 % interval of (VB - VA)/G1 is < 0.5, and VB < VA'. Otherwise it is refuted.
null: A' is the same samples with each converted row that is wrong abstaining instead of voting. This pure yield/ceiling account (grader-m06, f2-m02) predicts zero flips and a gain of VA' - VA. The scatter part is checked against a second Think-SFT sample: 16k-finished wrong rows from sample 1 against samples 2-3 give the base rate at which a wrong vote matches other wrong votes. RL's cap32 row plus 3 RL samples is the cross-model comparison.

statement: Think-SFT imitated teacher traces inside its ChatML template, opened by <think> and closed by a final answer after the thinking block. Where and how it states the answer is learned conditional on that template. On the raw template with the cue it reasons as well but sometimes misplaces the final answer (on the line after 'Answer:'), which v3 misses. Its own template restores the trained ending: more MATH-500 answers counted, unchanged reasoning length and cap behaviour on hard328.
claim: Think-SFT's own ChatML <think> template does not make it drift less: on hard328 at cap 32,768, the share of rows whose first 16,384 tokens contain a drift sign (switch into a non-Latin script or a repeated 50-token window) is the same as with the raw template and the cue. Only where the final answer is stated changes.
why_only_this: run-04/f2-m05 is the only other mechanism that talks about the template, and it predicts the opposite: in its own format Think-SFT samples a sharper, on-distribution distribution, so fewer long answers drift, while raw-template cue runs keep the drift. That mechanism needs native drift to be clearly lower; this one needs it unchanged, because the template only sets where the answer is stated and the model reasons as well either way. The rest say nothing about Think-SFT's template. They cover the RL direction split (round-10/weights-m06), how capped rows are rescored (run-08/f2-m02, round-09/grader-m06), seed scatter (round-09/grader-m01, run-08/f2-m01), cap-hit abstention in votes (run-08/f2-m06), the difficulty mix (round-09/grader-m04) and the stratum split of edits (round-10/problems-m04). None of them predicts any template effect on drift, in either direction.
computation: 1. Load the per-problem rows of the native cell (studies/rlneurons/results/native/hard328-01: Think-SFT, own chat format, cap 32,768; result-dd9239, 232 at 32k, 204 at 16k). Load the matched raw-template cue cell at the same cap (studies/rlneurons/results/cap32/sft_cue-01; its text rows are in cap32/rows-01 or rows-02, whichever holds the sft_cue rows: 230 at 32k, 207 at 16k, result-c8b994). Join the two on problem index, giving 328 pairs. Before going on, check that each cell's v3-right count matches its posted 32k and 16k count. 2. Cut every row to its first 16,384 generated tokens. Use the stored token ids if the rows have them. Otherwise tokenize the text offline with the Think-SFT tokenizer (allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Think-SFT), on CPU. Comparing at a common length means the native cell's longer answers cannot add drift chances. 3. On each cut row, compute the two drift signs exactly as analysis/drift.py defines them (the same code that produced studies/rlneurons/results/drift/describe-01): (a) the first token position where the text switches into a non-Latin script (CJK, Cyrillic and the rest, per drift.py's script rule); (b) the first position where a 50-token window repeats an earlier window. A row is drifted if (a) or (b) fires anywhere in the first 16,384 tokens. Before running, reproduce drift.py's planted tests (analysis/drift_test.py) and check that the raw-cue drift rate you get on thinkvote sample 0 matches describe-01's stored value for the same rows. 4. Primary statistic: D = (drifted share, native) - (drifted share, raw cue at cap 32k), in percentage points of 328. Get a 95 % interval by a paired bootstrap over problems (10,000 resamples, seed 0). 5. Null: the seed scatter of the same quantity within the raw-cue template. Take the four raw-cue samples in studies/rlneurons/results/thinkvote/hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01 (cap 16,384, so their rows already end at 16,384 tokens), compute each sample's drifted share with the same code, and report every pairwise difference and the largest one in absolute value, S_max. Also compute D against each of the four thinkvote samples, cutting the native rows to 16,384 tokens as in step 2. 6. Secondary checks, reported but not deciding: (i) cap hits at 16,384 and median tokens of finished rows, native against raw cue, which this mechanism says are unchanged; (ii) on the raw-cue rows that v3 grades wrong and that finished, the number whose next non-empty line after the last line reading 'Answer:' (case-insensitive, markdown stripped, nothing after the colon) is math-verify-equivalent to the gold answer. This mechanism says these are the only rows the native template recovers. 7. Report D with its interval, S_max, the four D values against the thinkvote samples, and the secondary numbers.
refuted_if: The native template drifts clearly less than the raw template with the cue: D is at most -2.0 points (about 7 of 328 rows fewer drifted), the upper end of its paired 95 % interval is below 0, and |D| is larger than S_max, the largest drift-share difference between two raw-cue samples.
threshold: D <= -2.0 percentage points of 328, with paired-bootstrap 95 % upper bound < 0 and |D| > S_max. If any of these fails, the claim holds. If D comes out positive, that also counts against f2-m05.
null: Seed scatter within one template. The drift-share differences between the four stored raw-cue samples (thinkvote hard328_sft1_cue_s4-01) set how large a template difference has to be to count. This is stronger than a random baseline: it is the same model, prompt and grader on a second base sample, so any native-minus-raw difference inside S_max is indistinguishable from re-sampling.
